sources.citation: Sumbuk, Kenneth Memson. 1999. Morphosyntax of Sare. PhD thesis, University of Waikato. xiii+335 pp. (hdl 10289/13888). Ch.1 with Chart 1.1 'The position of Sare within the Sepik area Papuan languages (Laycock 1973)'; 2.2.1 Stress (pp.40-42) for Sare/Kapriman only.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Read held by the project: the thesis describes Sare (Kapriman, kapr1245) only; p.2 'Of the Sepik Hill Family, to which Sare belongs, only Alamblak (Bruce 1984), has a comprehensive description'; the explicit stress rule (2.2.1, pp.40-42: secondary stress initial, primary stress final in disyllables and penultimate in longer words) is for Sare alone; nothing on this language.

sources.citation: Conrad, Robert & Ron Lewis. 1988. Some language and sociolinguistic relationships in the Upper Sepik region of Papua New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26 (Pacific Linguistics A-76), 243-273; and Conrad, Robert & Wayne Dye. 1975. Some language relationships in the Upper Sepik region of Papua New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 18 (Pacific Linguistics A-40), 1-35.
sources.note: Nothing. Lexicostatistics (Chenapian 35% cognate with Wogamusin, <=10% with anything else; 1975: 7-15% with Middle Sepik, 45-55 items compared) and sociolinguistics (village visited; population ~250 in 1988; Tok Pisin widely known). No phonology.

sources.citation: Summer Institute of Linguistics. 1983. Language Survey of Chenapian (two survey wordlists), as published in transnewguinea.org (Simon J. Greenhill, ed.), sources sil-1983a and sil-1983b; and Lexibank 'transnewguineaorg-chenapian'.
sources.note: Bare phonetic wordlists (~100 items each, e.g. head toapᵒ / tuwap, eye ǰinino / džinano, dog ogwara / gwara, cloud nəŋga). No stress marks anywhere (only háček and length dots occur as diacritics); no prose.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. & John Z'graggen. 1975. The Sepik-Ramu phylum. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 731-763. Canberra: ANU. Section 'WOGAMUSIN AND CHENAPIAN', pp. 743-744. hdl 1885/145150.
sources.note: Nothing. The whole Chenapian phonology is one sentence: the phonemes of Wogamusin (after Laycock 1965b) are /p t k b d g mb nd ŋg m n ŋ s h w r y a e i ə o u/ and 'those of Chenapian appear to be similar, but it is necessary to add /ñ/'; then two pronoun sets and five numeral classes 'with some of the Chenapian forms not fully established' and 'the data in Chenapian, at least, are fragmentary'. a full-text search for stress/accent in the Sepik-Ramu chapter finds no Chenapian statement (the p. 732 phylum-wide 'lack of complex suprasegmental systems' is not about Chenapian).

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1973. Sepik languages: checklist and preliminary classification (Pacific Linguistics B-25). Canberra: ANU. Entry 71 CHENAPIAN (Tsenap, Zenap), p. 21. hdl 1885/146478.
sources.note: No stress statement. Entry: 187 speakers, village Chenapian [CD 49W], 'Test DCL71 (Samuel/Chenapian). It is not completely certain whether this language belongs with this family, or in the Tama family of the Tama stock; typologically, however, it is close to Wogamusin.' No phonology reference is given (unlike entry 70 Wogamusin: 'Phonology Laycock (1965a)').

sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, not open: the recorded link is dead or did not deliver the file in two reading (2026-09-18, 2026-09-19); the linked copy could not be retrieved
sources.note: The only primary data on Chenapian beyond the 1975 half-page; Foley 2018 says these fieldnotes are all that exists. Laycock's elicitation sheets normally mark stress on transcribed words, so the notebook is the one place a Chenapian stress pattern could be read off (no prose statement expected). Access is 'Open (subject to agreeing to PDSC access conditions)': needs a free PARADISEC login in a browser; downloads athttps://catalog.paradisec.org.au/repository/DL2/043/DL2-043-Notebook_D34.pdfare an automated-access block-challenged to scripts.
